analysis.one_liner: Keeps old criminal records and arrests off the reports landlords use to screen renters.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on July 11, 2023, got no hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The Housing FIRST Act would stop the companies that produce tenant screening reports from including arrests, juvenile records, dismissed or resolved cases, and criminal convictions where the person has already completed their sentence. It would also force landlords who deny someone housing based on a screening report to tell the applicant the specific reasons within three days, and would wipe convictions off credit reports after seven years. The goal is to keep people with past criminal records from being shut out of rental housing for life.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters with any brush with the criminal justice system gain the most: the roughly one in three American adults with an arrest or conviction record could no longer be automatically rejected by a landlord over arrests, juvenile records, or sentences already served. People leaving jail or prison would get a fairer shot at stable housing, which research links to lower repeat-offense rates. Applicants denied housing would at least learn exactly why, and could demand to know where the information came from.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters with arrests or old convictions

how_it_helps.text: Bars tenant screening reports from including arrests, juvenile records, civil citations, cases resolved through diversion or drug court, convictions with completed sentences, and anyone on probation or parole [S2, S3].

Removes the exemption that let criminal convictions stay on credit reports indefinitely; under the bill, convictions would disappear from all consumer reports after seven years, like other negative information [S2, S3].

Requires landlords to notify a rejected applicant within three days, provide the report itself, and state the specific reasons for the denial, so applicants can challenge inaccurate or stale records [S2, S3].
Lets consumers find out which entity supplied damaging information on their report, making it easier to correct errors fed into tenant screening databases [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tenant screening companies would lose a major part of their product, since criminal history is a selling point of the reports they sell landlords. Landlords would lose access to criminal background information entirely when screening tenants, even for recent offenses where the sentence is finished, and would bear any added risk they attribute to that. Applicants and consumer agencies would bear the cost of policing compliance, since the Fair Credit Reporting Act is enforced mainly through complaints and lawsuits rather than automatic checks.

drawbacks.text: Landlords and screening firms argue the bill strips them of any ability to weigh criminal history, including convictions for serious offenses where the sentence is complete, raising safety concerns for other tenants and neighbors [S3].

Section 7 preempts state laws about how long information stays on reports, so a federal seven-year ceiling would override states that set different rules, including some stricter state protections [S3].

Section 8 applies the seven-year conviction limit to all consumer credit reports, not just tenant screening, which reaches further into background use than the bill's housing-focused title suggests [S3].
Enforcement under the Fair Credit Reporting Act relies on individual complaints and litigation, so landlords could keep screening informally and violations would be hard to detect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people with records, the benefit is concrete: stable housing is one of the strongest predictors of staying out of the criminal justice system, and the bill removes the automatic lifetime barrier of a completed sentence or old arrest. The costs are real but narrower: landlords genuinely lose information they say protects other tenants, and screening companies lose revenue. The bill is broadly drafted — the seven-year rule reaches all credit reports — which is more than a tenant-focused bill strictly needed and would have drawn pushback in committee. On balance it is a targeted consumer protection whose main burden falls on two concentrated interests rather than on ordinary renters.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Ayanna Pressley introduced the bill on July 11, 2023, with 16 Democratic cosponsors including Tlaib, Ocasio-Cortez, and McGovern [S1, S3, S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, which handles Fair Credit Reporting Act changes [S1, S5].
The action history shows nothing after that referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point in the 118th Congress [S5].
All 16 cosponsors were Democrats, and with Republicans holding the House majority and the committee chairmanship, the bill never moved [S4, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tenant screening companies and landlords are better off because the bill died: they keep full access to criminal history when screening tenants. People with arrest or conviction records are no better off than before and remain exposed to automatic denials of rental housing.

industries.industry: Tenant screening and background check companies
industries.note: These firms sell landlords reports built partly on criminal history data; the bill would strip arrests, juvenile records, and completed sentences out of that product, cutting a core selling point. Their interest in selling richer files runs against renters' interest in not being rejected over old records.

Landlords would lose all criminal-history information when screening applicants, including for recent convictions with completed sentences, and would owe rejected applicants specific written reasons. They say the information protects tenants and property; renters with records say it locks them out of housing permanently.

The bill removes the conviction exemption from the seven-year limit on all consumer credit reports, deleting data the bureaus currently sell and adding new duties when their reports are used for housing decisions.
